entries.note: An indeterminate amount of improvement supplies no shared standard for assessing the comparison.

entries.test: Public technical documentation and independent evaluations could establish whether Anthropic demonstrated recursive self-improvement or capabilities beyond improved LLM benchmark performance.
entries.note: The normalization strengthens 'has not done much more' into 'just' and drops the asserted purpose of the marketing.
This asserts the private purpose of the marketing; the valuation alone cannot establish that purpose.
He endorses a possibility, not a firm prediction. The normalization omits the proxy marketing campaign that is part of that scenario.
He explicitly says hyperscalers 'might be trying' to do this.
'Hard to see' expresses doubt rather than a firm prediction that normality will not return.
Cost pressures are measurable, but IPO dependence on 'myth, hype, and certainty' has no shared evidentiary threshold.
The relief is explicitly speculative; the comparison of corporate fears also concerns private attitudes.

entries.test: Public financial disclosures showing revenues, operating costs, subsidies, and customer retention could establish whether the two business models cover their costs.
entries.note: The surrounding financial argument gives 'do not work' a plain economic reading.

entries.test: Public billing changes, subscription economics, customer spending reductions, and financial results could test whether withdrawing subsidies caused the described deterioration.
entries.note: The passage attributes the deterioration to changing subsidy arrangements.

entries.test: Representative public evidence of customer acceptance and churn when AI is priced to cover its costs would test whether a majority refuse to pay.
entries.note: This is a firm majority prediction with no deadline.

entries.test: Public customer complaints, spending reductions, and reporting on the companies' pricing decisions could establish whether customer resistance prompted planned drastic cuts.
entries.note: The price-cut mechanism gives the bubble language a concrete meaning.

entries.test: A documented enterprise AI deployment with positive returns after accounting for its costs would refute the assertion that nobody could demonstrate ROI.
entries.note: The universal assertion is testable despite its emphatic phrasing.

entries.test: Public studies or customer records comparing efficiency practices and spending under subsidized subscriptions and usage billing could test the claimed behavioral effect.
entries.note: The billing transition is supplied by the surrounding discussion.

entries.test: Public revenue breakdowns, customer deployment reports, and spending-control documentation could establish how much of Anthropic's revenue increase came from experimental customers lacking spend visibility.
entries.note: 'Most' weakens 'the vast majority'; the source also specifies lack of clear visibility.

entries.test: Public compute commitments and financial projections could test the $358 billion requirement, while growth and solvency records following a slowdown could test the predicted failure.
entries.note: The revenue requirement is dated 2029. The separate prediction of failure after any slowdown has no stated deadline.

entries.test: Industry financial results, insolvencies, and closures following the proposed token price cuts would test the prediction of fatal financial damage.
entries.note: In context, 'deadly' predicts financial failure rather than merely expressing disapproval.

entries.test: Public inference margins and revenues before and after the discounts, together with their size, would test whether the cuts eliminated margins and reduced revenues.
entries.note: The revenue question is sarcastic but conveys his own asserted financial consequence.
The predicted revenue collapse is explicitly 'likely' and depends on the planned cuts occurring.
'Every chance' presents a possible consequence of price cuts.
The customer response is hedged. The separate assertion that DeepSeek-level cuts would be fatal is firm and could be checked separately.

entries.test: Public pricing announcements, customer demand evidence, and inference cost trends could distinguish customer resistance from efficiency gains as the driver of cuts.
entries.note: This asserts an economic cause that can be investigated through public evidence.

entries.test: Public financing announcements, closing records, and cost disclosures could test the conditional $230 billion total and its relationship to rising costs.
entries.note: The proposition omits 'assuming the rounds completely close.' The source explicitly links fundraising to increasing costs.

entries.test: Reproducible subscription usage tests, rate limits, and contemporaneous API prices could establish the token value available under each $200 plan.
entries.note: The dollar amounts refer to API-priced usage, not necessarily the providers' actual compute costs.
He infers private confidence from pricing behavior; he does not establish a publicly testable confidence measure.

entries.test: SemiAnalysis's published subscription limits and margin calculations could establish the gross margin at 25% utilization under the assumed 75% token margin.
entries.note: This is a calculation under a stated assumption, not a future prediction.
'Not real businesses' is a dismissive characterization, not a claim that the companies do not legally exist.

entries.test: Public provider cost trends, customer prices, and measured economic returns could test the claims that generative AI is not getting cheaper or delivering value commensurate with costs.
entries.note: The proposition weakens 'not ... remotely commensurate' to 'not commensurate.' The passage includes concrete economic assertions despite its rhetoric.

entries.test: Independent longitudinal measures of real-world task performance and documented unsubsidized customer returns could test the asserted absence of improvement and exclusive revenue sources.
entries.note: The categorical denial of measurable improvement outside AI benchmarks is falsifiable.

entries.test: Published mathematical results, task-level token measurements, and provider cost records could test whether hallucinations are guaranteed and increase costs at unprofitable prices.
entries.note: The proposition explicitly links hallucinations to additional token consumption and customer costs.

entries.test: Public usage, market-share, and deployment records after a lab stops training could establish whether its models lose practical relevance.
entries.note: The prediction has a stated antecedent but no deadline.

entries.test: Public financial breakdowns separating training, inference, and other expenses could establish whether removing training expenses would leave the companies unprofitable.
entries.note: The surrounding argument supplies a concrete accounting reading; the behavioral counterfactual is his supporting rationale.
The normalization turns a claim about buyers' expectations into a categorical claim of spending without results. 'Disconnected from any real work' also lacks a shared classification test.
The source infers present private plans from remarks; it does not firmly predict implemented cuts. The normalization adds an explicit causal explanation.

entries.test: Public provider financials and large-scale deployment evaluations available at publication could establish whether cheap open-source models had demonstrated profitability, sustainability, and competitive performance.
entries.note: The proposition drops sustainability and broadens comparison with the labs' 'more-complex LLMs' to the companies generally.
He expresses skepticism about a shift rather than firmly asserting that no shift exists.

entries.test: Public workforce replacement records and controlled studies of productivity and software delivery could test all three assertions.
entries.note: The absence claims have ordinary empirical readings despite the evaluative word 'compelling.'

entries.test: An independently verified AI-produced research response containing no hallucinations would refute the universal claim.
entries.note: This describes an asserted general property of current AI research outputs.
'Most' weakens 'the vast majority.' The asserted explanation concerns customers' private feelings and motives.
This is a dismissive characterization of their economics, not a literal corporate-status claim.
'Might' explicitly leaves the viability claim uncertain.

entries.test: Public customer uptake and churn when offered unsubsidized token billing could establish whether the vast majority refuse to pay for their usage.
entries.note: In context, this firmly predicts behavior if users must pay the full cost; 'would never' is not a probability hedge.

entries.test: Public revenues and expenses excluding training, together with customer responses to cost-covering price increases, could test the claimed economics and price sensitivity.
entries.note: This asserts current financial inadequacy and a present constraint on pricing.

entries.test: Applicable accounting standards and the nature of the training expenditures could establish whether they qualify as cost of goods sold or capital expenditure.
entries.note: He asserts that training costs are cost of goods sold; the normalization changes that accounting assertion into a recommendation.

entries.test: Public SpaceX deal terms and Anthropic's financial results immediately after price cuts or customer churn could test the discount dependence and predicted losses.
entries.note: The source alleges an attempt to appear profitable, not an established profitable quarter. It specifies discounts for the first two months.
The categorical assertion concerns whether an internal plan exists, not merely whether either company has published one.

entries.test: Public operating results, infrastructure costs across chip platforms, and customer responses to pricing could test the asserted unprofitability and price sensitivity.
entries.note: The passage makes a present economic claim, not merely an insult.

entries.test: A sustained publicly documented reversal of adverse costs and customer price resistance would refute the claim that the trend cannot be reversed.
entries.note: This is a firm undated claim of irreversibility.
The combined characterization judges management and business legitimacy without specifying a financial outcome or standard of recklessness.

entries.test: Public cost trends, profitability, and customer uptake following added data-center capacity could test the asserted absence of economic benefits.
entries.note: The normalization extends the profitability and willingness-to-pay claims to VC funding, which the source only says will not make them 'real businesses.' The core claim denies a causal effect of expansion.
This explicitly recommends pausing development.
'If they fail' narrows 'if anything happens to them.' Absorption is explicitly described as likely.
The normalization omits the predicted end of the startup dream. It combines an assumed future collapse with the explicitly hedged possibility that these are the last hypergrowth startups.
The proposition generalizes the actors and turns the contextual leverage argument into a firmer conclusion. Whether the companies privately care about Anthropic's survival is not publicly settleable.

entries.test: Public evidence of Anthropic's business collapse, such as insolvency or cessation of operations, would test the prediction.
entries.note: 'I believe will' expresses a firm expectation here, with no deadline.
